items.name: Kafka topics, partitions and offsets
items.explanation: Kafka keeps messages in an ordered log per topic, split into partitions. Each partition has a leader that takes writes, and followers that copy it.

assumedBy.quote: This is because, by default, Kafka clients communicate only with the partition leader, which has a 67% probability of residing in a different AZ.

items.name: Regions and availability zones
items.explanation: A cloud region is made of several availability zones, which are separate data centres with their own power and network. Spreading across zones survives a zone failure, and traffic between zones is billed.

assumedBy.quote: The Grab platform is primarily hosted on AWS cloud, located in one region, spanning over three Availability Zones (AZs).

items.name: SQLite and write-ahead logging
items.explanation: SQLite is a database that lives in one local file. In write-ahead logging mode, writers append to a log file while readers keep reading the main file, so reads and writes can overlap.

assumedBy.quote: One of the first things we did was enabling write ahead logging for our SQLite database.

items.name: Kubernetes StatefulSets
items.explanation: A StatefulSet runs pods that keep a stable identity and their own storage. If a pod restarts, it comes back with the same volume and its data.

assumedBy.quote: We stored the SQLite database on an EBS-backed volume attached to each Kubernetes StatefulSet pod.
